subject: orthopaedics
title: Injuries of the shoulder girdle and arm

steps.tx: The **shoulder** is the most frequently dislocated large joint. Anterior dislocation accounts for roughly 97 percent of cases, and the humeral head lies in front of the glenoid. Usual mechanism is a fall on an outstretched hand with abduction, external rotation and extension. The **axillary nerve** is the nerve most commonly injured in anterior dislocation, because its short fixed course round the surgical neck makes it vulnerable to traction.

steps.tx: Recurrent dislocation follows a traumatic first episode in many young adults. Three essential lesions are classic: the **Bankart lesion**, a tear of the anterior labrum off the anterior glenoid rim, and the **Hill-Sachs lesion**, a compression defect on the posterolateral humeral head. Capsular laxity is the third. Tests such as the apprehension and relocation tests help detect instability.

steps.tx: Operative options for recurrent instability include the **Bankart repair**, which reattaches the labrum, and the **Putti-Platt operation**, which shortens and tightens the anterior capsule and subscapularis. The **Bristow-Latarjet operation** reinforces the antero-inferior capsule by transferring a coracoid graft. Hill-Sachs lesions are relevant to surgical planning.

steps.tx: **Axillary nerve** injury causes deltoid and teres minor weakness and loss of sensation over the lower deltoid, the regimental badge area. Fracture of the **surgical neck of the humerus** is the classic cause. Radial nerve palsy follows **fracture shaft of the humerus**, often at the junction of the middle and distal thirds, where the nerve is tethered at the spiral groove.

steps.tx: **Clavicle fracture** is most common at the junction of the middle and outer thirds. The medial fragment is pulled up by sternocleidomastoid, and the lateral fragment drops because of gravity and pectoralis major. Distal third fractures with coracoclavicular ligament rupture (Neer type II) are usually managed surgically, while non-displaced distal fractures are splinted. A figure of eight bandage is classic for clavicle fractures.

steps.tx: Three **high-yield pearls** anchor this chapter. A **Holstein-Lewis fracture** is a spiral fracture of the distal humeral shaft that threatens the **radial nerve**. **Luxatio erecta**, an inferior glenohumeral dislocation, puts the **axillary nerve** and vessels at risk. Fracture healing relies on the **periosteum**, which supplies the **osteoblasts** forming new bone. Use the lesion map and the nerve map together when you revise.
